title: This Viper Grows a Fake Spider on Its Tail, and Birds Fall for It

scenes.text: This snake's tail ends in a spider. The spider isn't real.
The first one was collected in Iran in 1968. Scientists took the lump on its tail for a deformity, maybe a tumour.
Only in 2006 was it named as a new species: the spider-tailed horned viper. The knob carries long scales that look just like legs.
The snake lies still against the rock and moves only its tail, so the spider seems to scurry. A bird drops in for an easy meal.
The strike takes about a fifth of a second.
One more twist. The adults were only seen catching migrating birds. Not one local bird was caught. They seem to know that spider.

description:
A viper in western Iran has a tail tip shaped like a spider, with a knob for the body and long scales for legs, and it wiggles it to lure birds within reach.
The first specimen, collected in 1968, was written off as deformed; the species was only described in 2006. Filmed strikes take about 0.2 seconds, and in one study the adults caught only migratory birds, mostly warblers, while resident birds stayed away.
Would you have fallen for it?

first_comment: Young vipers were seen catching lizards; only the adults take birds. Which animal has the best lure: this viper, the anglerfish, or the snapping turtle?
